prayer.text: Saint William of York, pray for us.

cues.text: A Contested Election
William Fitzherbert, sometimes called William of Thwayt, was born in York around the end of the eleventh century.
He was the son of Herbert of Winchester, treasurer to King Henry I, and Emma, believed by tradition to have been a half-sister of King Stephen.
By about 1130, William was already canon and treasurer of York.
In 1141, the king's influence secured his election as archbishop, a choice bitterly opposed by Cistercian monks and archdeacons.
They preferred Henry Murdac, a Cistercian abbot, and accused William of simony and undue royal pressure.
Archbishop Theobald of Canterbury refused to consecrate William while the appeal to Rome remained unsettled.
St. Bernard of Clairvaux, the most influential churchman of the age, opposed him vigorously.
He wrote letter after letter to Rome on Murdac's behalf.
Consecrated, Then Deposed
In 1143 the pope ruled that William could be consecrated if he cleared himself of the bribery charges, which he did, to the apparent satisfaction of Rome at the time.
He was duly consecrated archbishop and governed York for several years.
But when Bernard's own protege, Eugene III, became pope, the case was reopened.
In the winter of 1145 to 1146, Eugene declared William's original consecration invalid and suspended him from office.
By 1147, he had been formally deposed in favor of Murdac.
Years of Prayer at Winchester
Rather than contest the ruling by force or continued appeal, William withdrew to Winchester, where his own father had served as treasurer.
He gave himself over to prayer and mortification, living as a private monk for the better part of six years.
Whatever the justice of the charges brought against him, later tradition treated them as politically motivated rather than genuinely deserved.
That tradition was more sympathetic than the record can fully verify.
William's response to his deposition was received by contemporaries as a mark of real humility rather than mere resignation.
Restoration and a Sudden Death
Murdac died in October 1153, and within weeks so did William's chief remaining opponent, St. Bernard, who had died some months earlier that same year, along with Pope Eugene III.
With the case's principal antagonists gone, William appealed to the new pope, Anastasius IV, who restored him to York and granted him the pallium.

William returned to his see and, tradition holds, showed particular kindness to the very Cistercians who had worked hardest against him, promising full restitution to Fountains Abbey for wrongs done during the dispute.
His restoration proved brief.
Within a month of his return, William died suddenly, so suddenly that some among his own household suspected poison.
No formal inquiry resolved the question, and the precise cause of his death remains, in the sober judgment of history, unknown.
Miracles and Canonization
Reports of miracles at William's tomb began almost immediately and continued for decades, including accounts of the dead being raised to life through his intercession.

In 1227, Pope Honorius III canonized him, and in 1283 his relics were translated to a magnificent shrine behind the high altar of York Minster, where they remained a center of pilgrimage until the shrine's destruction during the English Reformation.
Legacy
William's story does not resolve neatly into either scandal or vindication.
The historical record leaves the original charges against him genuinely uncertain.
The Church's devotion grew not from a tidy exoneration, but from how he bore both disgrace and restoration.
We recognize in William something every believer wrongly accused has had to learn the hard way.
The only answer to injustice that does not corrode the soul is the same one William gave from his brief months back in York: not triumph over one's accusers, but mercy toward them.
